summary: German physician Samuel Hahnemann invented homeopathy in the 1790s after dosing patients and family with poisons; the story then follows its modern harms, from Hyland's belladonna teething tablets in the US to patients who died forgoing real treatment.

evidence.note: Masonic lodge initiation and exposure to alchemy and spiritism
1790 cinchona bark self-experiment, the first consequential act
sets up practice prescribing poisons like strychnine and mercury
1835 Nuremberg double-blind salt water trial against homeopathy
last years as a socialite in France, death in 1843
homeopathic diarrhea trial on children in Honduras
Hyland's teething tablets linked to infant seizures and deaths
CAM lobbying, ACA section 2706 and the 1938 Copeland law on FDA oversight
2018 case report of belladonna toxicity from Topricin cream
2017 death of an Italian girl treated homeopathically for an ear infection
Penelope Dingle's death from untreated cancer in Perth, Australia

notes: Hahnemann and homeopathy are both primary: part 1 is his life, part 2 the practice's modern harms. main_span follows Hahnemann (1790 cinchona test to 1843 death); covered_span runs to the 2018 Topricin case because part 2 narrates homeopathy's direct harms at length. The host says Hahnemann was not really a bastard. Penelope Dingle's birth year is not given. FR is a short segment on his final years.
